identification.summary: Iranian nation-state threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Peach Sandstorm (formerly HOLMIUM), whose activity overlaps with public reporting on APT33, Elfin and Refined Kitten [S1]. Microsoft assesses that it operates on behalf of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and runs long-term intelligence-gathering operations [S2]. Since 2023 its typical tradecraft has been large-scale password spraying followed by cloud-focused post-compromise activity in Microsoft Entra ID and Azure, including command and control (C2) hosted in fraudulent Azure subscriptions [S1][S2]. Earlier Mandiant (FireEye) reporting describes a group focused on aviation and on energy and petrochemical targets in Saudi Arabia, the United States and South Korea [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: cyber espionage since at least 2013, with the earliest TURNEDUP compile timestamp dated April 2013 [S3]. Microsoft cites a 2019 password-spray wave and spraying since at least February 2023 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Peach Sandstorm (formerly HOLMIUM). Microsoft states overlap, not identity, with APT33 (Mandiant), Elfin (Symantec) and Refined Kitten (CrowdStrike) [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as APT33 (G0064) [S7]. Facts from APT33/Elfin-era reporting (2013-2019) stay attributed to their original vendors and are not merged into Microsoft's Peach Sandstorm findings. Microsoft notes that other Iranian groups, including Smoke Sandstorm, have used similar techniques, so tradecraft alone does not identify this actor [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Islamic Republic of Iran. Microsoft assesses that Peach Sandstorm operates on behalf of the IRGC [S2]. Mandiant (2017) assessed that APT33 works at the behest of the Iranian government [S3].
attribution.confidence: These are vendor assessments only. Microsoft bases its IRGC assessment on victimology and operational focus and states no confidence level [S2]. Its 2023 report says the spray campaign is 'likely' used for intelligence collection in support of Iranian state interests [S1]. Mandiant uses hedged language and calls APT33 'most likely government sponsored' [S3]. Press coverage of FalseFont says Microsoft did not tie that activity to a specific Iranian government entity [S6]. This pass found no US government attribution naming Peach Sandstorm or APT33.
attribution.basis: Victimology and operational focus [S2]. Activity in late May and June 2023 fell almost entirely within 09:00-17:00 Iran Standard Time [S1]. Mandiant also cited activity in a UTC+04:30 time zone and on Iran's Saturday-Wednesday workweek, use of Iranian hacker tools and hosting providers, Farsi artifacts in DROPSHOT/SHAPESHIFT, and the persona 'xman_1365_x', which open sources linked to the Nasr Institute [S3].

objectives: Intelligence collection in support of Iranian state interests [S1][S2]. Targeting of satellite, defense, government and oil-and-gas organizations shows interest in military, space and energy information [S1][S2]. Mandiant judged the aviation focus may serve Iran's interest in military and commercial aviation, and the petrochemical focus its energy-sector interests [S3]. Earlier reporting also shows possible preparation for disruption. Mandiant found the SHAPESHIFT wiper in APT33's toolset but had not seen it used destructively [S3]. Microsoft in 2019 (as reported) suggested that targeting industrial control system (ICS) suppliers might be aimed at physically disruptive access, though it said motive remained unclear [S5].

sectors: Oil and gas, energy and petrochemical [S2][S3]
regions: Global (2023 spraying of thousands of organizations) [S1]
targeting.notes: Microsoft lists earlier targeting across aviation, construction, education, energy, financial services, healthcare, government and telecommunications [S1]. Peach Sandstorm used compromised education-sector accounts to buy Azure infrastructure, so universities are both victims and enablers [S2].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft-reported (2023-2024) capabilities: high-volume password spraying from TOR IPs with a 'go-http-client' user agent, and exploitation of public proof-of-concept exploits for Zoho ManageEngine (CVE-2022-47966) and Confluence (CVE-2022-26134) [S1]. Post-compromise, Microsoft reported Entra ID reconnaissance with AzureHound and ROADtools, and persistence through Azure Arc, new or abused Azure subscriptions and AnyDesk [S1]. It also reported the custom tunneling tool EagleRelay, a Golden SAML attack in March 2023, and DLL search-order hijacking [S1]. The custom multi-stage backdoor Tickler (2024) used Azure C2 nodes under azurewebsites.net in fraudulent subscriptions, Run-key persistence and SMB lateral movement [S2]. LinkedIn personas have been used for reconnaissance and possible social engineering since at least November 2021 [S2]. The FalseFont backdoor (late 2023) offers remote access, file execution and data exfiltration to C2 (as reported) [S6]. Mandiant-reported (2017) tooling includes the DROPSHOT dropper, TURNEDUP backdoor, SHAPESHIFT wiper, NANOCORE, NETWIRE and ALFA Shell, plus recruitment-themed spear-phishing with .hta files and domains impersonating Boeing, Alsalam Aircraft, Northrop Grumman Aviation Arabia and Vinnell Arabia [S3].

campaigns.name: Aviation and petrochemical espionage (Mandiant APT33)
campaigns.summary: A US aerospace organization was compromised from mid-2016 to early 2017. A Saudi conglomerate with aviation holdings and a South Korean petrochemical company were targeted with job-recruitment spear-phishing that delivered TURNEDUP. Domains impersonated defense and aviation firms.

campaigns.name: Narrowed password spraying against ICS suppliers (Microsoft, CYBERWARCON)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft (as reported) said the group narrowed spraying to about 2,000 organizations a month. About half of its top 25 targets were makers, suppliers or maintainers of ICS equipment.

campaigns.name: LinkedIn persona operations
campaigns.summary: Fake LinkedIn profiles posing as students, developers and recruiters targeted higher education and satellite sectors from at least November 2021 to mid-2024.

campaigns.name: Global password spray campaign
campaigns.summary: From February to July 2023, password spraying hit thousands of organizations. Follow-on activity included Entra ID reconnaissance, Azure Arc persistence and EagleRelay, a March 2023 Golden SAML intrusion, and data exfiltration in a small number of cases.

campaigns.name: FalseFont backdoor against defense industrial base
campaigns.summary: Microsoft (as reported) saw Peach Sandstorm attempting to deliver the new FalseFont backdoor to individuals at defense industrial base organizations. First use was observed in early November 2023.

campaigns.name: Tickler backdoor and Azure C2 operations
campaigns.summary: From April to July 2024, Tickler was deployed against satellite, communications equipment, oil and gas, and government targets in the US and UAE. Password spraying hit defense, space, education and government organizations in the US and Australia. Microsoft disrupted the fraudulent Azure subscriptions.

diamond.adversary: IRGC-aligned Iranian operators, per Microsoft's assessment [S2]. Mandiant linked the persona 'xman_1365_x' to the tooling [S3].
diamond.capability: Password spraying, public N-day exploits, Entra ID and Azure abuse (Golden SAML, Azure Arc) and custom backdoors (Tickler, FalseFont, TURNEDUP), plus the SHAPESHIFT wiper [S1][S2][S3][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: TOR exit IPs for spraying [S1]. Fraudulent Azure subscriptions bought with compromised education accounts and used for C2 [S2]. Earlier, dynamic-DNS domains impersonating aviation and defense firms [S3].
diamond.victim: Satellite, defense/DIB, government, oil and gas, aviation and pharmaceutical organizations in the US, Gulf states, Australia, Europe and South Korea [S1][S2][S3][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection for Iranian state interests [S1]. Microsoft tied a 2019 spray wave to rising US-Iran tensions [S1]. Mandiant linked the aviation focus to Iran's interest in military aviation capability [S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing cloud identity (Microsoft 365 and Entra ID) with weak passwords and no MFA, unpatched ManageEngine and Confluence servers, and cloud tenant trust relationships [S1][S2].

gaps: No US government attribution or advisory naming Peach Sandstorm or APT33 was located; IRGC sponsorship rests on Microsoft's assessment [S2].
FalseFont details come from press coverage of Microsoft's December 2023 social-media disclosure, which did not disclose the delivery method; no Microsoft blog post was opened [S6].
The Microsoft 2019 CYBERWARCON findings come from Axios coverage; no Microsoft primary document was found [S5].

A 2026 CloudSEK advisory (seen only in search excerpts; fetch failed) claims APT33 deployed a 'Shamoon 4.0' wiper against about 15,000 Saudi energy workstations in January 2026. It is single-source, unverified and NOT included as fact.
No Microsoft or Mandiant primary reporting on Peach Sandstorm activity in 2025-2026 was found. A November 2025 Brandefense forecast was seen but not used.
Mandiant's link between the persona and the Nasr Institute, and any ties to Shamoon/StoneDrill, remain unproven. Mandiant said it had not directly seen APT33 carry out destructive operations [S3].
Trend Micro (2019 narrow-targeting botnets) and Recorded Future (2019, more than 1,200 domains) reports were not opened in this pass.
It is unclear whether any ICS supplier targeted in 2019 was breached, or whether any damage resulted [S5].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is cloud identity (Entra ID and Microsoft 365 tenants) at satellite, space, defense-industrial-base and government organizations, along with Azure subscriptions and internet-facing ManageEngine and Confluence servers [S1][S2]. STEP 2 (effects): Weak passwords and missing MFA on DIB and space contractor tenants offer an indirect path to DoD program data. Compromised university accounts let the adversary stand up infrastructure on trusted cloud domains that blend with normal traffic [S2]. STEP 3 (adversary model): The pattern runs from LinkedIn persona reconnaissance, to low-and-slow password spraying from TOR, to Entra ID reconnaissance (AzureHound/ROADtools), to persistence (Azure Arc, AnyDesk, Golden SAML), to a custom backdoor (Tickler or FalseFont) with Azure-hosted C2, to SMB lateral movement and exfiltration [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued credential-based intelligence collection against DIB, satellite and government tenants that rises with US-Iran tension [S1][S2]. MDCOA is using ICS-supplier and energy footholds for disruptive or wiper operations, given SHAPESHIFT in the toolset and 2019 ICS-supplier targeting [S3][S5]. Candidate indicators: bursts of failed sign-ins from TOR with 'go-http-client' user agents; unexpected Azure Arc enrollment or new Azure subscriptions; outbound traffic to newly created azurewebsites.net hosts; new SharePoint.exe Run-key entries; and AnyDesk installs on servers [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: identity telemetry (sign-in logs, conditional access failures, federation/SAML changes) from DIB and space-sector partners should be fused with DoD network sensing, because this actor's primary access vector is cloud identity, not the DODIN perimeter [S1][S2]. (2) Authorities: most targets are contractor- or university-owned tenants and Azure infrastructure, so response depends on partners and cloud providers (Microsoft disrupted the fraudulent subscriptions), not on DoD action [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: Prioritize MFA and password-spray detection for satellite, space and weapons-program contractors, and track defended-asset dependence on vendors such as ICS suppliers [S2][S5][S6]. (4) Coordination: Coordinate with DC3/DIB CS and cloud-provider threat intelligence, and raise the watch level during periods of US-Iran tension, which Microsoft linked to earlier spray waves [S1].
